The Brown surgeonfish Acanthurus nigrofuscus attains a maximum recorded total length of 21 centimeters [Li = 21 centimeters], a size that places it among the smaller members of the surgeonfish family. Field surveys conducted on the Great Barrier Reef indicate that individuals reach this asymptotic length after several years of steady somatic growth. The egg diameter of this species is approximately 0.7 millimeters, and based on this spherical dimension, the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This minute mass reflects the pelagic larval strategy common among acanthurids, where a high fecundity and small offspring size are traded off against extensive larval dispersal. During the early developmental stages, the fertilised ovum undergoes rapid cleavage and transitions through a yolk-sac larva phase that relies on endogenous reserves before the onset of exogenous feeding. The initial weeks of life are therefore characterized by a period of intense yolk utilization and the gradual development of the feeding apparatus necessary for a planktonic existence.

Reproductive maturation in Acanthurus nigrofuscus occurs at a total length of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters], a size that corresponds to the onset of gonadal activity and the ability to participate in spawning aggregations. The wet weight at this pubertal transition is estimated at 39.3 grams [Wwp = 39.3 grams], derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species. This body mass at the onset of sexual maturity represents approximately one-fifth of the ultimate adult mass, suggesting that individuals allocate considerable resources to continued somatic growth even after becoming reproductively viable. In contrast, the maximum adult wet weight recorded for the species reaches 206 grams [Wwi = 206 grams], a value consistent with the asymptotic length and the allometric scaling parameters reported for Acanthurus nigrofuscus. This ultimate mass is achieved only after several years of sustained feeding on benthic algae, with growth rates slowing considerably as individuals approach their maximum size.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Acanthurus nigrofuscus was quantified under controlled laboratory conditions, with a mean value of 9% [GSI = 9%] recorded when the water temperature was maintained at 16.7 °C [T = 16.7 °C]. Seasonal fluctuations in water temperature are known to modulate the reproductive cycle of this species, with peaks in spawning activity coinciding with the warmer summer months when primary productivity is highest.

Longevity estimates for Acanthurus nigrofuscus are based on mark-recapture studies and otolith increment analysis, which indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. These records were obtained from populations inhabiting reef systems where the mean annual water temperature is approximately 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], a thermal regime typical of tropical Indo-Pacific waters. Such an extended lifespan, remarkable for a fish of this body size, positions the Brown surgeonfish as a relatively slow-living species among its acanthurid congeners. The combination of a long reproductive lifespan and iteroparous spawning strategy allows individuals to buffer against years of poor recruitment or unfavorable environmental conditions. This life-history pattern, characterized by delayed senescence and sustained reproductive output, is thought to be an adaptation to the unpredictable variability in larval survival that characterizes coral reef ecosystems.

Comparative analysis of life-history traits across the genus Acanthurus reveals that Acanthurus nigrofuscus exhibits a notably high longevity relative to its ultimate body mass, with some individuals surviving for a quarter of a century (25 years) [am = 25 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C]. This contrasts with more short-lived surgeonfish species that reach sexual maturity more rapidly but have correspondingly shorter reproductive windows. The gonadosomatic index of 9% [GSI = 9%] was measured at a water temperature of 16.7 °C [T = 16.7 °C]. Population modeling efforts suggest that the species' persistent abundance on many Indo-Pacific reefs is attributable to this conservative life-history strategy, where moderate annual fecundity is coupled with high adult survivorship and multiple spawning events across the extended lifespan. Understanding how these physiological parameters respond to ongoing ocean warming represents a pressing conservation priority for this ecologically important herbivore.
